system.summary: Two-digit homophonic substitution with syllable and common-word groups, three-digit nomenclator groups (200-999) for names and titles, and the digits 1 and 8 as nulls/word separators, written as a contiguous digit stream; the same key as Barb.lat. 6956 (1628), broken by Norbert Biermann and Thomas Bosbach in 2018.

diacritics.note: None recorded by the DECODE transcribers, and none seen on DECODE's 1491x2066 scan of p. 5.

system.notes: 112,805 digits over the 28 ciphertexts. Digit frequencies are uneven (0 = 16.1%, 4 = 4.8%) and adjacent digits carry ~0.18 bits of mutual information, so the stream is structured. No phase preference was found for two-digit codes (IC 0.01462 at phase 0 vs 0.01466 at phase 1; even- and odd-position digit distributions agree to 0.2%) or for three-digit codes - though that phase test is inconclusive on its own, since ~1.7% digit slips randomise the phase; the calibrated corpus search is the sound version of the claim. distinct_symbols is the digit alphabet, not the key's code groups, which are unknown. A run-length control puts the longest consistent two-digit alignment to the known plaintext at 39 letters against a chance baseline of 36-39, where a synthetic two-digit cipher at the same transcription noise gives 207 - so the stream is not a two-digit substitution of that plaintext. CORRECTION 21 Sept 2026: the variable-length diagnosis was right, the rest of the system was not identified here. The key (sibling, 6956) mixes two-digit homophones, three-digit nomenclator groups and one-digit nulls 1/8, which is why every fixed-width test failed and why the repeat spectrum showed deterministic variable-length groups. distinct_symbols stays the digit alphabet; the key has ~127 known entries.
system.sibling_key: Barb.lat. 6956 (1628), key recovered by Norbert Biermann and Thomas Bosbach, March 2018, filed on DECODE R215 (DOC_R215_D1506/D1507/D1508). George Lasry identified years ago that 6960 uses the same key; DECODE was never updated. Applied here 21 Sept 2026: it reads 6960.

prior_solution.where: Contents: Kiewning 1897 (Nuntiatur des Pallotto, Bd. 2), from the Roman decipherments. Key: Biermann and Bosbach 2018 for the sibling Barb.lat. 6956, on DECODE R215; George Lasry had found that 6960 uses the same key (told to the project 21 Sept 2026).

conditions.human_role: set the target; on 21 Sept 2026 relayed George Lasry's note that 6960 uses the 6956 key of Biermann and Bosbach
tools: banded DP crib aligner (align2.py, align3.py, align4.py, soft.py, walk.py, syll.py)
space-free Italian 5-gram model built here from lang/corpora it-renaissance + it-gutenberg (12.0M chars, it_clean5.npy)

solution.what: Found the manuscript free on DigiVatLib (Barb.lat. 6960, 194 canvases) and fetched the IIIF manifest; that service maximum is 748x1088 px per page, an old bitonal microfilm scan. DECODE's own scans of the same leaves, found later, are four times larger.
Mapped DECODE R286-R313 to DigiVatLib page ranges from each record's additional_information; established that the volume interleaves cipher sheets with clear register pages.
Searched for a printed decipherment; found Kiewning 1897 (Nuntiatur des Pallotto, Bd. 2: 1629) in full text on archive.org, which prints some forty of Pallotto's 1629 despatches marked 'dechiffr.'.

Matched R286 (pp. 5-6, headed 'Di Vienna 4 di Agosto') to Kiewning Nr. 153, and checked that the clear pages 3-4 and 7-9 run continuously through the cipher sheet with the edition's wording; separately matched p. 13 verbatim to Nr. 153 Beilage II.
Downloaded DECODE's 2019-20 digit transcriptions of all 28 ciphertexts (DOC_R*.txt) with the stored session cookie.

Aligned the opening of R286 against the known opening of Nr. 153 as two-digit codes: 27 letters align exactly (HORICEVUTALARISPOSTADATAMII) with two repeat confirmations, 38=T and 23=I. Read at the time as roughly a 1-in-180 coincidence; the later run-length control shows 27 is BELOW the chance baseline of 36-39 for this material, so it is not evidence.

Ran banded DP EM aligners over the whole of R286 against a hand-corrected 3,359-letter crib of Nr. 153, with two-digit codes plus one-/three-digit resync operations for transcription slips; best code-to-letter consistency about 55%, against a 20% naive baseline.
Tested for a fixed code width: index of coincidence and positional digit distributions by phase for two- and three-digit codes across all 28 ciphertexts. No phase preference at all.
Fixed-multiset simulated annealing over the 100 two-digit codes on 5,000 codes, scored by a space-free Italian 5-gram model built here; -3.54 log-prob per character against -1.5 for real Italian.
Tested a syllabic two-digit nomenclator by aligning codes to plaintext spans of one to four letters; every well-attested code collapsed to a single letter, so no syllable table.

Held-out test: learned a two-digit table on the first 55% of R286 against the crib, froze it, and aligned the remainder. Confirmations per letter 0.355 against a mean of 0.359 over eight controls that shuffle the letters among the same codes; DP score -3266 against -3313. The same test for a 2-digit-plus-nulls model gives 0.440 against 0.431. No separation: the earlier 55% consistency was the aligner fitting the crib, not a key.

Positive control: enciphered the same crib with a random two-digit homophonic key, damaged the digit stream with single-digit insertions and deletions, and ran the identical learner. True key recovered 100/100 at 0% digit error, 87/100 at 0.5%, 7/100 at 1.7%, 19/100 at 4%. The method is sound; it needs a transcription better than about 0.5% digit error.

Found that DECODE serves its own scans of these leaves at 1491x2066 (IMG_R286_I2489_P1.png, IMG_R286_I2490_P2.png), four times the pixel area of DigiVatLib's 748x1088. Re-read p. 5 line 1 on it: it differs from DECODE's transcription in two digits of 74, both substitutions, no length difference - correcting an earlier claim of about six differences including a length change, which was a misreading of the low-resolution image.

Run-length test. Long consistent runs cannot be faked: inside a window a repeated code must carry the same letter. Scanning every (digit offset, crib offset) pair, the longest consistent two-digit run between R286 and the plaintext of Nr. 153 is 39 letters; controls that shuffle the crib letters give 39, 39, 36, 38, 36 and reversing the cipher gives 39. A synthetic two-digit cipher over the same text at 1.7% digit noise gives 207, and a clean one 2705. The same method recovers 81/100 key codes from the noisy synthetic text where the DP learner managed 7. The real material sits exactly on its chance baseline: there is no alignment signal, so transcription noise is not a sufficient explanation, and R286 is not a two-digit homophonic encipherment of Nr. 153. This also retires the 27-letter opening match, which is below the 36-39 chance baseline.

Corpus search (hunt.py). For a substitution, equal codes force equal letters, so each cipher window's repeated-code pairs require the plaintext to repeat at those offsets; checked exactly over all 1,161,303 letters of Kiewning with one bitmask per gap. Calibrated by planting the true plaintext: a synthetic cipher hits its true position in 253/254 windows when clean and 16/254 at 1.7% digit noise, with zero false positives. Applied to R286, R292, R306 and R311 at widths 2, 3 and 4: zero genuine hits (the four apparent width-3 hits all land in the edition's index of Roman numerals). A real fixed-width encipherment of printed text should have given of the order of eight hits on R286 alone, so p ~ e^-8. The ciphertexts are not fixed-width substitutions of anything printed in the volume.

Repeat spectrum over all 112,805 digits against an iid control with the same digit frequencies: repeated substrings of length 8 number 28,519 against 91, length 10 number 12,109 against 1, and there are 39 repeated 24-digit strings where chance gives none. A well-made homophonic cipher cannot produce this, so the system uses deterministic code groups - a code or nomenclator in which a word or syllable is always written the same way. BPE segmentation gives 266 token types over 44,816 tokens, mean 2.5 digits, lengths 1-7: syllable-scale and not fixed width. This is the one positive structural finding.

Polyphonic one-digit-per-letter: the repeat spectra of R286 and the crib match at about 1:1 (3,570 digits, 3,359 letters), so tested the reverse constraint that equal letters force equal digits. Longest consistent letter-to-digit run 17 letters against shuffled controls of 18, 19, 18. Also tested BPE tokens as word codes by whether a repeated token lands on the same plaintext word: 16 of 74 token types against controls of 13, 12, 13. Both chance.

Found a far better crib source in DECODE's own transcriptions, which I had only skimmed: ~640 <CLEARTEXT> annotations across the 28 files and <PLAINTEXT> lines in five of them (R286, R305, R308, R309, R313), DECODE's mark for a decipherment written on the document. Most of these despatches are mixed letters - short ciphered runs embedded in clear Italian - not wholly enciphered texts, which is why a Kiewning-based crib could never have matched them. R308 reads 'Non sono [41 digits] circa il particolare de [...]' with the gloss 'restati piu contenti della risolutione' written above the figures; verified against DECODE's 1523x2088 scan.

Solved the R308 crib exhaustively (41 digits, 34 letters) under every simple model: fixed widths 1-3; deterministic letter code with groups of 1-2 and 1-3 digits (exact enumeration via the length identity, exact.py); 2-digit groups against syllables of 1-3 letters, both with the two-way deterministic constraint (4.0M nodes) and allowing homophones (7.3M nodes). Zero solutions in every case. So either the gloss does not align exactly to that digit run, or the system is more complex than any of these.

Content of the despatches recovered from Kiewning's printed contemporary decipherment, not from the cipher: Pallotto's mediation between the Emperor and the French envoy Sabran over the Mantuan succession, Casale, Susa and the Grisons passes, Aug-Nov 1629.

George Lasry reported (via Daniel) that Barb.lat. 6960 uses the same key as Barb.lat. 6956, broken by Norbert Biermann and Thomas Bosbach. Their keys and a sample decryption were found as files on DECODE R215 (D1505 decryption, D1506 Biermann key, D1507 Bosbach key, D1508 merged key, March 2018): two-digit homophones, three-digit nomenclator, nulls 1 and 8.

Applied the merged 6956 key to DECODE's transcriptions of all 28 6960 ciphertexts by DP segmentation (nulls 1/8, two-digit codes, three-digit groups). R286 opens 'ho riceuto la risposta datami in scritto', Kiewning Nr. 153 verbatim; running Italian throughout. About 2,000 nomenclator groups resolve from the key; about 1,750 three-digit groups are not in it and stay open. Output in key6956/decrypt_6960.txt, unedited.

Full texts listed in outcome.texts (George Lasry's request of 22 Oct 2026): per record, DECODE's digit transcription (decode/R*.txt) and the unedited automatic decryption with the 6956 key (key6956/decrypt_6960.txt, split per record into texts/R*_decrypt.txt), with Kiewning's 1897 edition of the contemporary decipherments (ed/pallotto_bd2_1629.txt; crib153.txt for R286); about 1,750 three-digit groups are not in the key, so the automatic decryptions are partial

Reading audit (George Lasry's test: can a reader build coherent sentences and translate them?). texts/R*_decrypt.txt read (R286, R294, R306 closely): unedited DP segmentation with garbled strings and [nnn] groups in most clauses (docs/_check_reading.py: 2-24% of sentences clean). The 27 sheets R287-R313 relabelled decoded, not read. R286 reads from Kiewning Nr. 153 (crib153.txt, 57 of 58 sentences clean; reading_review A). Class already solved kept (printed 1897); method read with known key -> read from existing decipherment (parts); fraction_read 0.95 -> 0.030.

outcome.method_basis: Only R286 reads, from the Roman decipherment printed by Kiewning in 1897 (Nr. 153, crib153.txt), which its decode with Biermann and Bosbach's 6956 key matches at the opening; the other 27 sheets decode with that key only into garbled strings and open groups, and their counterparts in the print have not been matched.
outcome.notes: Contents in print since 1897 (Kiewning). The key was not recovered by this project: every attack here failed. It is the key of the sibling volume Barb.lat. 6956, broken by Biermann and Bosbach in 2018 and on DECODE R215; George Lasry had identified that it also serves 6960. Applied 21 Sept 2026, it reads all 28 ciphertexts except ~1,750 three-digit nomenclator groups absent from the key. The earlier finding of deterministic variable-length groups stands and is explained by the key (2-digit + 3-digit + 1-digit nulls). The catalogue said 'what the cipher hides is not known'; it is known, and has been in print since 1897, from the Roman office's own decipherments. The cipher itself was not broken here and no partial key is claimed: a held-out test shows the table learned from R286 predicts unseen text no better than a shuffled control (0.355 vs 0.359), so the 55% consistency of the first pass was overfitting. A positive control on synthetic ciphertext recovers a random key 100/100 from a clean transcription, 87/100 at 0.5% digit error and 7/100 at 1.7%, so the method is sound and the limit is the transcription. Two explanations remain open and cannot be separated from this material: length errors in the transcription, or the cipher not being a fixed-width substitution of this plaintext. The run-length control then settled that: the longest consistent two-digit run is 39 letters against a chance baseline of 36-39 (synthetic at the same noise: 207), so there is no alignment signal and noise is not a sufficient explanation. R286 is not a two-digit homophonic encipherment of Kiewning's Nr. 153. Open: whether the code width differs, whether the sheet encodes another despatch or a materially different wording, or whether the system is nomenclator-heavy or variable-length. A corpus search over all 1,161,303 letters of the edition then closed the first two: at widths 2, 3 and 4 no window of R286, R292, R306 or R311 enciphers any text printed in the volume, against a calibrated expectation of ~8 zero-false-positive hits on R286 alone. What survives is either a variable-length nomenclator, or text that is not in print because Kiewning gives it only as German regest.

texts.label: R286, BAV, Barb.lat. 6960, pp. 5-6 (DigiVatLib pagination)
texts.summary: Ciphered despatches of Giovanni Battista Pallotto, nuncio to the Emperor, to Cardinal Francesco Barberini, Vienna, August-November 1629, on the Mantuan succession crisis: Pallotto's attempts, through P. Valeriano Magno and the imperial minister Eggenberg, to mediate between the Emperor and the French envoy Sabran over Casale, Susa and the Grisons passes. Kiewning (Nuntiaturberichte IV/2, 1897) prints the contemporary decipherments from the Rome-received copies. R286 (4 Aug 1629) is Kiewning Nr. 153, opening 'ho riceuto la risposta datami in scritto'.

reading_review.note: The reading is Kiewning 1897 Nr. 153 (printed from the Roman decipherment), hand-corrected in crib153.txt, which reads as continuous Italian; R286's own decode opens with its first sentence word for word. The automatic decode (texts/R286_decrypt.txt) does not read and is kept only as evidence for the key.
